literal: He was granted the viscounty of Linzi and made Governor of Guangning, then died.
idiomatic: He was enfeoffed as Viscount of Linzi, appointed Governor of Guangning, and died.

literal: Xieli had two sons, Huaishun and Cien, who still lived in Qingzhou of Song.
idiomatic: Xieli left two sons, Huaishun and Cien, who remained in Song's Qingzhou.

literal: Huaishun, because his father had entered Wei, did not take office.
idiomatic: Huaishun, his father now in Wei, declined office.

literal: When Wei conquered Qingzhou, Huaishun brought Xieli's coffin back to Qingzhou—or so it is said.
idiomatic: When Wei took Qingzhou, Huaishun bore Xieli's remains home, or so the tale runs.

literal: Chong's younger brother Ni, courtesy name Daochang.
idiomatic: Chong's younger brother Ni, style Daochang.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Xiaowen's reign he was Director of the Southern Ministry and held the post fourteen years.
idiomatic: In Xiaowen's early reign he headed the Southern Ministry for fourteen years.

literal: The southern provinces were then full of troubles, and litigants filled his gate.
idiomatic: The south seethed with lawsuits; suitors packed his doorway.

literal: Ni was scholarly, slow, and unable to decide; he slept in a daze all day.
idiomatic: Ni was learned, hesitant, and incurably drowsy—he dozed the day away.

literal: Li Kan, Deng Zongqing, and others were called sharp and discerning, yet in the end both were executed.
idiomatic: Li Kan, Deng Zongqing, and the like were famed for keen judgment—and both were killed.

literal: Of the remaining dozen or so, some were dismissed and some spared; only Ni in the end preserved himself.
idiomatic: A dozen others were driven out or spared; Ni alone kept his skin.

literal: People said at the time, "Truly dull, truly dim—and in the end he was saved."
idiomatic: A saying ran, "Thick-headed, half asleep—and yet he survived."

literal: Later he was enfeoffed as Duke of Huashan, entered court as Grand Inner Steward, and died.
idiomatic: He was later made Duke of Huashan, rose to Grand Inner Steward, and died.

literal: His son Zunian inherited the title.
idiomatic: His son Zunian succeeded to the title.

literal: Zunian's younger brother Yun, courtesy name Luohan, had considerable refinement and held the post of Governor of Southern Yanzhou.
idiomatic: Zunian's brother Yun, style Luohan, was a man of taste and became Governor of Southern Yanzhou.

literal: He was impeached for taking bribes from Du Qian, commandant of the Jingshan garrison in his province, and for seizing official silk, then dyeing and substituting it—there was fraud in the exchange.
idiomatic: He took gifts from Du Qian, his Jingshan garrison chief, and official silk he recolored and swapped—censors brought charges.

literal: He was spared when an amnesty was proclaimed.
idiomatic: An amnesty spared him.

literal: He died in office and was posthumously made Governor of Yu, with the posthumous name Literary and Illustrious.
idiomatic: He died in post and was posthumously Governor of Yu, styled Literary and Illustrious.

literal: His eldest son was Xin.
idiomatic: His eldest son was Xin.

literal: Xin, courtesy name Yuanjing, in youth was devoted to study and could recite books; each day he used the height to which he could raise his hand above a stacked set of volumes as his measure.
idiomatic: Xin, style Yuanjing, studied relentlessly and knew books by heart; daily he gauged progress by how high his hand reached over a stack of texts.

literal: Together with Wang Yanji of Taiyuan he visited the Prince of Anfeng, Yanming.
idiomatic: He and Wang Yanji of Taiyuan called on Prince of Anfeng Yanming.

literal: Yanming sighed in admiration.
idiomatic: Yanming marveled at them.

literal: The Grand Guardian, the Prince of Runan, Yue, engaged him as Riding Attendant.
idiomatic: Grand Guardian Prince of Runan Yue took him on as Riding Attendant.

literal: By old custom, when a prince went out the riding attendants wore martial dress and carried blades in attendance.
idiomatic: Custom required that when a prince rode forth his attendants follow in martial dress with blades.

literal: Xin was ashamed of this and would never stand in the procession.
idiomatic: Xin found it shameful and refused to fall into line.

literal: Yue loved roaming and would sometimes gallop through the night; Xin would abandon him and return.
idiomatic: Yue loved reckless travel and might ride all night; Xin would leave him and go home.

literal: Yue then ordered the cavalry to ride ahead and personally drove them on.
idiomatic: Yue set the horsemen before him and lashed them forward himself.

literal: Xin dropped the reins and sat with hands clasped high, letting the horse go where it would; those beside him said he was mad and arrogant.
idiomatic: Xin let the reins hang and sat with folded hands, wherever the horse pleased; attendants called him insolent and unhinged.

literal: Yue said, "My house's hope rests on this worthy alone—he cannot be blamed."
idiomatic: Yue said, "The honor of my house is this man—leave him be."

literal: Yue several times scattered coins on the ground and ordered his staff to scramble for them; Xin alone did not pick any up.
idiomatic: Yue would fling coins for his men to snatch; Xin never stooped.

literal: Yue again scattered silver coins with his eyes on Xin, and then Xin took one.
idiomatic: Yue tossed silver pieces and watched Xin—at last Xin took one.

literal: When Yue drank with his staff he would rise and move his own couch; everyone rushed to help, but Xin alone held his tablet and stood back.
idiomatic: At wine Yue would shift his own seat; all rushed to assist, but Xin clasped his board and stood apart.

literal: Yue darkened his face and said, "I am the emperor's grandson, son, brother, and uncle—now I rise to move my couch myself; why this arrogance?"
idiomatic: Yue's color changed: "I am imperial grandson, son, brother, uncle—and I lift my own couch; why do you lounge?"

literal: He replied, "Yuanjing's rank and standing are slight and low—not enough to make Your Highness bow and view ritual form; how dare I, as a prince's staff member, follow a groom's labor?"
idiomatic: He answered, "Yuanjing is too small a man for Your Highness to bend ritual toward; shall a prince's officer play stable boy?"

literal: Yue apologized to him.
idiomatic: Yue begged his pardon.

literal: Everyone at the table drank deep in high spirits;
idiomatic: The company drank themselves merry;

literal: Xin rose first and lay down in a side room; though summoned repeatedly he would not come.
idiomatic: Xin left early and stretched out in a side chamber; calls could not fetch him.

literal: Yue then went in person to summon him and said, "You cherish your talent yet neglect your lord of the house—can that be called humane?"
idiomatic: Yue sought him out: "You prize your gifts and scorn your host—is that humanity?"

literal: Xin said, "King Zhou of Shang sank in debauchery; his fall came all at once."
idiomatic: Xin said, "King Zhou drowned in pleasure; his end arrived in a blink."

literal: "The lord of the house is arrogant by his own neglect—how should his staff bear the blame?"
idiomatic: "When the host forgets himself, why should the staff answer for it?"

literal: Yue laughed loudly and left.
idiomatic: Yue laughed and walked away.

literal: Later he was made Editorial Assistant.
idiomatic: He was later made Editorial Assistant.

literal: As warfare gradually rose he meant to flee to the sea's edge.
idiomatic: War spread; he planned to escape to the coast.

literal: The Attendant-in-chief Li Yanzhi and the Yellow Gate Gentleman Wang Zunye, cherishing so noted a man, would not allow an outer appointment and had him made Right Outer Troops Attendant in the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: Li Yanzhi and Wang Zunye, unwilling to lose a luminary to the provinces, secured him a post as Right Outer Troops Attendant in the Masters of Writing.

literal: He went out as chief administrator of Guang province and thus escaped the disaster at Heyin.
idiomatic: As chief administrator of Guang he missed the slaughter at Heyin.

literal: He was moved to Governor of Donglai.
idiomatic: He was transferred to Governor of Donglai.

literal: In those years famine was severe and many ate one another; Xin worked hard to relieve hidden suffering and saved many.
idiomatic: Famine turned men to cannibalism; Xin labored in secret charity and kept multitudes alive.

literal: In youth Xin and Xing Shao of Hejian had both been guests of Yuan Luo; when Xin governed Donglai, Shao brought his whole household to him.
idiomatic: Young Xin and Xing Shao of Hejian had shared Yuan Luo's table; when Xin held Donglai, Shao came with all his kin.

literal: The people of the commandery, because Shao was a cousin of Xing Gao, were about to seize him with armed men.
idiomatic: Locals, knowing Shao was cousin to the rebel Xing Gao, meant to take him by force.

literal: Xin shielded him with his own body and cried, "If you want Zicai, take me first!"
idiomatic: Xin threw himself over Shao and shouted, "Want Zicai? Take me first!"

literal: Shao was thus spared.
idiomatic: Shao was saved.

literal: Xin was fond of pure talk; his words were never shallow or vulgar.
idiomatic: Xin loved refined discourse and never spoke cheaply.

literal: In Donglai he captured a man who had killed his traveling companion; questioned, the man would not confess.
idiomatic: In Donglai he caught a murderer of his fellow traveler who would not confess under interrogation.

literal: Xin said to him, "That man did not return—yet you came back unharmed; how will you clear yourself?"
idiomatic: Xin told him, "Your companion never came home—you walked back whole; how do you prove innocence?"

literal: When Xing Shao later saw Wen Xiang, he repeated the line for amusement.
idiomatic: Later Shao told Wen Xiang the quip for a laugh.

literal: When Xin heard of it he went to Shao and said, "You do not understand creation."
idiomatic: Xin heard and confronted Shao: "You do not know fate."

literal: Returning, he told others, "Zicai ought to die—I cursed him to the bone."
idiomatic: He told others, "Zicai deserves death; I damned him to the marrow."

literal: Before long, slandered, he was demoted to Governor of Yangping.
idiomatic: Soon slander banished him to Governor of Yangping.

literal: In the commandery he won a name for achievement.
idiomatic: There he earned repute for his work.

literal: Wen Xiang told others, "Wang Yuanjing owes me much strength—because I teased him so often, in official business he has become a fine governor of two thousand households."
idiomatic: Wen Xiang said, "Yuanjing thrives on my jests—hounded into office, he became a true governor."

literal: When Emperor Wenxuan of Qi took the throne, Xin was made Minister of the Seven Armies.
idiomatic: At Qi Wenxuan's accession Xin became Minister of the Seven Armies.

literal: For participating in deliberations on ritual he was enfeoffed as Baron of Yijun.
idiomatic: He helped shape ritual and was made Baron of Yijun.

literal: Once there was a cluster speaking Xianbei; Cui Ang playfully asked Xin, "Do you understand any of this?"
idiomatic: A knot of men spoke Xianbei; Cui Ang teased, "Do you follow any of it?"

literal: Xin said, "Louluo, louluo—it is truly hard to grasp.
idiomatic: Xin said, "Louluo, louluo—beyond me entirely.

literal: What they sing now, ran-dyed, seems to mean our sort."
idiomatic: Their current chant, ran-dyed, sounds like 'us fellows.'"

literal: Wenxuan, because Xin was loose and eccentric and not talent for ordering the age, cursed, "Fine house, vile man!"
idiomatic: Wenxuan judged Xin frivolous, no statesman, and snarled, "Noble gate, wretched body!"

literal: Others also slandered him, saying, "Wang Yuanjing constantly sighs that the water transport ought not to have been cut off."
idiomatic: Slander added that Yuanjing lamented the end of the canal.

literal: The emperor grew angrier still and issued an edict: "Yuanjing was by nature a mediocrity, without merit from the first, yet early girded with office and so walked the clear path.
idiomatic: The emperor's rage peaked; the edict read, "Yuanjing was always mediocrity, never meritorious, yet early robed and on the high road.

literal: Starting from the capital region he leapt to Junior Tutor.
idiomatic: From the inner provinces he vaulted to Junior Tutor.

literal: Soon he wore the dragon-pattern sword and opened the book of belt and whetstone.
idiomatic: Soon he bore the dragon sword and the covenant stone.

literal: Speaking of his measure of capacity—how did he reach here?
idiomatic: By what measure did he climb so high?

literal: He ought to have cleared his heart and striven in himself, repaying the throne one part in ten thousand.
idiomatic: He should have purified himself and repaid the throne in the smallest measure.

literal: The Masters of Writing are the root of the hundred offices; all affairs return there.
idiomatic: The Masters of Writing anchor the bureaucracy; all business flows there.

literal: Yuanjing judged arbitrarily as he pleased; authority and favor rested in himself.
idiomatic: Yuanjing judged capriciously; power and grace were his alone.

literal: He could make the straight crooked and the bent like a bowstring.
idiomatic: He bent straight lines and strung curves.

literal: He harmed government and injured the public—where was honor's name?
idiomatic: He wounded the state—where was righteousness?

literal: He feigned the taste of a guest officer and loved to chant frivolous verses.
idiomatic: He played at salon wit and dabbled in light verse.

literal: He called himself imitating the barbarian Chu and claimed to exhaust their airs and styles.
idiomatic: He styled himself a mimic of northern song and boasted mastery of its tones.

literal: Taking that as his strength—what else is worth taking?
idiomatic: That was his gift—what else had he?

literal: If this is not disciplined, how will the future be made reverent?
idiomatic: If this goes unpunished, what discipline remains?

literal: His titles and ranks in life should be stripped.
idiomatic: Strip his living ranks.

literal: Thereupon he was moved to Youzhou as a commoner.
idiomatic: He was exiled to Youzhou as a commoner.

literal: Xin accepted fortune and misfortune without changing his conduct.
idiomatic: Through fortune and ruin Xin did not bend.

literal: Before long he was recalled and, by imperial order, escorted Xiao Zhuang to Liang to be enthroned.
idiomatic: Soon he was summoned back to conduct Xiao Zhuang to Liang as king.

literal: He was made Grand Master of Splendorous Light and acting Minister of the Imperial Ancestors.
idiomatic: He was given Splendorous Light rank and acting charge of the Imperial Ancestors.

literal: The emperor, enraged at Linzhang Magistrate Ji Ye and Gentleman of the Palace Interior Li Wenshi, gave Ye to Xue Fengluo and Wenshi to Cui Shishun as slaves.
idiomatic: Wenxuan, furious at Ji Ye of Linzhang and Li Wenshi, gave Ye to Xue Fengluo and Wenshi to Cui Shishun as bondsmen.

literal: Zheng Zimo privately urged Xin, "Since antiquity no court gentleman has been made a slave."
idiomatic: Zheng Zimo whispered to Xin, "Never in history was a courtier enslaved."

literal: Xin said, "Jizi became a slave—how can you say there was none?"
idiomatic: Xin answered, "Jizi was enslaved—how say never?"

literal: Zimo then reported Xin's words to Wenxuan, adding, "Wang Yuanjing compares Your Majesty to King Zhou of Shang."
idiomatic: Zimo told Wenxuan, adding, "Yuanjing likens Your Majesty to King Zhou."

literal: Yang Yin lightly excused him.
idiomatic: Yang Yin softened the matter.

literal: The emperor told Yin, "Wang Yuanjing is your doctoral teacher—your every word is Yuanjing's teaching."
idiomatic: The emperor told Yin, "Yuanjing is your teacher; all you say is his lesson."

literal: Later, when the emperor drank deep with the court, Xin pleaded illness and did not attend.
idiomatic: Later, at a court revel, Xin claimed sickness and stayed away.

literal: The emperor sent riders to seize him; they found him swaying on his knees, chanting poetry, and he was beheaded before the throne; the corpse was cast into the Zhang waters.
idiomatic: Riders seized him—he was rocking on his knees, reciting verse—and he was cut down before the throne and thrown into the Zhang.

literal: At the end of Tiantong he was posthumously made Minister of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: In late Tiantong he was posthumously Minister of the Masters of Writing.

literal: He left a collected works in twenty juan.
idiomatic: His collected writings ran twenty juan.

literal: His son Yan inherited.
idiomatic: His son Yan succeeded.

literal: He died as Governor of Yan commandery.
idiomatic: He died as Governor of Yan.

literal: Xin's mother was of the Cui clan of Qinghe, learned and with cultured instruction.
idiomatic: His mother was Lady Cui of Qinghe, scholarly and strict in nurture.

literal: She bore nine sons, all refined and accomplished; the age called them the Nine Dragons of the Wang house.
idiomatic: Nine sons, each polished; the world called them the Nine Dragons of Wang.

literal: Xin's younger brothers Hui, Zhao, Xi, and Hao were the most famed.
idiomatic: His brothers Hui, Zhao, Xi, and Hao were best known.
